page10_img_table3.png.title: Top‑1 accuracy and dataset share for CONCAT vs OTHER classes
page10_img_table3.png.description: This table compares DEEPMERGE’s top‑1 synthesis accuracy and the proportion of the dataset for two categorical classes of resolutions: CONCAT (resolutions that are a pure concatenation AB or BA) and OTHER (all other interleavings). CONCAT samples make up 26.88% of the dataset and achieve 44.40% top‑1 accuracy, while OTHER samples constitute 73.12% and achieve 29.03% top‑1 accuracy. In other words, DEEPMERGE is more accurate on CONCAT-style resolutions, although the majority of examples belong to the OTHER class where accuracy is lower.

page7_img_code_b.png.title: Resolved code region showing inserted baz() between print_time calls
page7_img_code_b.png.description: A short resolved-region excerpt delimited by <BOF> and <EOF> showing four lines of code: "let time = new Date();", "print_time(time);", "baz();", and "print_time(time);" (with an ellipsis indicating preceding context). This resolution includes an inserted call to baz() between two print_time invocations and a declaration using let for time; according to the paper this baz() insertion (and surrounding context changes such as var→let) does not correspond directly to edits in A or B, making localization of the true resolution region ambiguous for the dataset extraction algorithm.

page8_img_1.png.title: Comparison of Top-1 and Top-3 resolution synthesis accuracy across methods
page8_img_1.png.description: A table reporting exact (line-for-line, token-for-token) top-1 and top-3 synthesis accuracies on the held-out test set for DEEPMERGE and three baselines. DEEPMERGE achieves 36.50% top-1 and 43.23% top-3 accuracy, substantially outperforming the heuristic ScanMerge (4.20% top-1, 7.43% top-3) and an off-the-shelf Seq2Seq model (2.3% top-1, 3.3% top-3). The semi-structured JSFSTMERGE baseline attains 3.7% top-1 accuracy and has no top-3 entry (N/A), consistent with it producing a single resolution output. The table summarizes that DEEPMERGE produces correct first-ranked resolutions far more often than the alternatives under the strict exact-match evaluation.

page1_img_1.png.title: Unstructured three-way merge examples: successful merge and conflict
page1_img_1.png.description: A four-column table showing Base (O: base.js), Variant A (a.js), Variant B (b.js), and the merged Resolution (m.js) for two numbered examples. In example (1) the base contains “y = 42;”, A adds “x = 1;” above that and B adds “z = 43;” below; the unstructured diff3 merge produces a combined resolution with x = 1; y = 42; z = 43; (both edits preserved). In example (2) A inserts “x = 1;” before the unchanged y line while B inserts “z = 43;” before the same y line; because these independent edits fall in the same diff3 slot, diff3 reports a CONFLICT even though the changes do not semantically interfere.

page10_img_table4_right.png.title: Top-1 and Top-3 accuracy by input representation
page10_img_table4_right.png.description: The table compares five Merge2Matrix input representations and reports DEEPMERGE’s Top-1 and Top-3 synthesis accuracy for each. Naïve (concat) is worst (Top-1 9.62%, Top-3 14.09%), Linearized improves modestly (15.25% / 19.95%), and the prior LTRE edit-aware format sits between (23.37% / 29.21%). The aligned variants that encode edit-aware alignments perform best: Aligned Naïve achieves 27.41% / 32.22%, and the Aligned Linearized representation yields the highest accuracy at 36.50% Top-1 and 43.23% Top-3, demonstrating that edit-aware, aligned summarization substantially boosts resolution synthesis performance.

page10_img_fig1.png.title: Precision, Recall, and F1 vs. Confidence Threshold for DEEPMERGE
page10_img_fig1.png.description: Line chart showing DEEPMERGE’s top‑1 precision (blue), recall (green), and F1 (red) as a function of the model confidence threshold (0.0–0.9). Precision rises steadily with higher thresholds (≈0.4 at 0.0 to ≈0.8+ by 0.9) while recall falls (≈0.36 at 0.0 down to ≈0.1 at 0.9); 95% confidence intervals are indicated by the dashed lines around each curve. The F1 score peaks around thresholds 0.4–0.5 at about 0.46, and at threshold 0.5 the authors report precision ≈0.72 and recall ≈0.34, illustrating the trade-off used to choose operating points that favor high precision with acceptable recall.

page3_img_1.png.title: Three-way merge conflict example showing inputs A, B, O and resolved R
page3_img_1.png.description: The figure shows a diff3 conflict on the left with markers (<<<<<<< a.js, ||||||| base.js, =======, >>>>>>> b.js) and the three versions’ code; a.js (A) has: "let b = x + 5.7", "var y = floor(b)", "console.log(y)"; base.js (O) has: "var b = 5.7", "var y = floor(b)"; b.js (B) has: "var y = floor(x + 5.7)". On the right the same content is presented as a merge tuple with boxed A, O, B and the resolved R which contains two lines: "var y = floor(x + 5.7)" (from B) and "console.log(y)" (from A). This illustrates a non-trivial resolution that reuses and reorders lines from the inputs (no new lines), matching the paper’s running example where R takes the first line from B and the third line from A.

page7_img_code_a.png.title: diff3 conflict showing competing 'x' assignments in a.js vs b.js
page7_img_code_a.png.description: A three-way diff3 conflict fragment using standard markers: <BOF> and <EOF> frame the file, with unchanged context lines "var time = new Date();" and "print_time(time);". Between the markers, <<<<<<< a.js shows A’s edit "x = foo();", ||||||| base.js denotes the common/base section, ======= separates versions, and >>>>>>> b.js shows B’s edit "x = bar();". The identical print_time(time); line appears both before and after the conflict region, illustrating extraneous surrounding edits that can make it hard to unambiguously localize the developer’s resolved region (the example in the paper is used to motivate that localization is non-trivial).

page5_img_1.png.title: DEEPMERGE pipeline: Merge2Matrix encoder with pointer-style decoder
page5_img_1.png.description: The diagram shows DEEPMERGE’s end-to-end flow: a diff3 conflict (left) with three inputs A, B, and O — each line annotated (e.g., <1,A>, <2,A>, <1,O>, <1,B>, <3,A>) — is transformed by Merge2Matrix into an edit-aware matrix embedding. That embedding is summarized by a bi-directional encoder (producing z_n) and fed to a decoder that iteratively outputs indices (pointer-style tokens) into the set of input lines (including a STOP token), with decoder hidden states h_m guiding each selection. The purple arrow highlights an example selection of line <1,B> during decoding; the final resolved snippet (green box) is constructed by copying lines from inputs (here <1,B> then <3,A> producing "var y = floor(x + 5.7)" and "console.log(y)"). This visual emphasizes DEEPMERGE’s design choice to synthesize resolutions by reusing and reordering existing input lines via an edit-aware representation and pointer-based generation.

page6_img_1.png.title: Aligned Linearized Merge2Matrix edit-aware encoding example
page6_img_1.png.description: The figure shows a concrete three-way merge snippet (left) and how Merge2Matrix converts the three tokenized inputs into an edit-aware input matrix (right). Tokenized variants A', AO', B', and BO' are aligned to produce two edit sequences Δ_AO = align(A,O) and Δ_BO = align(B,O), which are visualized as streams of edit-operation tokens (= for unchanged, + for insertion, - for deletion, ↔ for replacement, and ∅ for padding). These two edit sequences are embedded and then combined via the learnable linearize_θ (illustrated with ⊗) to produce the fixed-size D-dimensional matrix X^T = linearize_θ(Δ_AO, Δ_BO), which is the Merge2Matrix representation fed into DEEPMERGE’s encoder.

page7_img_algo_1.png.title: Algorithm to Localize and Filter Merge Tuples from Conflict and Resolved Files
page7_img_algo_1.png.description: The figure shows pseudocode for Algorithm 1 which extracts labeled merge tuples (A,B,O,R) from a diff3 conflict file C (with conflict markers) and the developer-resolved file M. The top-level procedure LocalizeMergeTuples iterates over each conflict, calls LocalizeResRegion(C,M,i) to find the resolution R for that conflict, skips unresolved or trivial cases (where R is nil or exactly equals A, B, or O), and only adds tuples whose resolution lines are a subset of the lines in A or B. LocalizeResRegion computes conflict character start/end positions (spos, epos), builds a prefix (prfx) and suffix (sffx) around the conflict, and uses MinimalUniquePrefix to find the smallest prefix/suffix that uniquely identify the resolved region in M; if both bounds are found it returns the corresponding slice M[n-s:e], otherwise nil. Helper procedures MinimalUniquePrefix(x,y) (returns start position of the minimal non-empty prefix of x that appears uniquely in y) and Lines(p) (returns the set of lines of program p) are specified for clarity.

page2_img_1.png.title: diff3 conflict format and concrete example
page2_img_1.png.description: The left side diagrams the diff3 conflict template: an unchanged prefix, the opening marker <<<<<<<, the lines edited by A, a ||||||| marker identifying the affected lines from the common base O, a ======= separator, the lines edited by B, the closing >>>>>>> marker, and an unchanged suffix. The right side gives a concrete instance labeled with file names: <<<<<<< a.js followed by “x = 1;”, then ||||||| base.js with “z = 43;”, then ======= and >>>>>>> b.js with “y = 42;”. The figure illustrates how diff3 presents the three versions (A, O, B) of a single diff slot so that overlapping edits (here three different assignment lines) are exposed as a merge conflict requiring manual resolution. The paper refers to this format to explain how diff3 aligns two-way diffs into slots and why independent edits in the same slot can trigger conflicts.

page9_img_1.png.title: DEEPMERGE top-1 accuracy by merge size
page9_img_1.png.description: This table reports DEEPMERGE’s top-1 synthesis accuracy (threshold = 0, i.e., no confidence filtering) broken down by total number of lines in the conflicting region. For merges of 1–3 lines accuracy is 78.40%, for 4–5 lines 56.50%, for 6–7 lines 37.04%, for 8–10 lines 10.87%, and for merges with more than 10 lines 2.93%. The numbers show a steep decline in exact-match accuracy as conflict size increases, consistent with the paper’s observation that DEEPMERGE performs best on small merge regions (≤3 lines).

page9_img_2.png.title: DEEPMERGE synthesis accuracy vs. merge size (Top-1/Top-3 and cumulative proportion)
page9_img_2.png.description: Line chart showing DEEPMERGE’s top-1 (blue) and top-3 (green) synthesis accuracies plotted against merge input size in lines (x-axis 1–20), with the red curve on a secondary axis giving the cumulative proportion of merges of that size. Accuracy is high for very small merges (around 0.78 for 3-line merges) and then falls off rapidly as merge size increases, with both top-1 and top-3 tracking closely and becoming low for larger sizes. The red cumulative curve shows that most merges are small (about 58% are size ≤7), explaining why overall performance is dominated by small inputs; accuracy for merges ≤7 lines is roughly 61% (top-1) as reported in the paper. The plotted accuracy lines are jagged at some sizes, indicating variability due to smaller sample counts at particular merge lengths.
